President Trump says Alaska Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola should suffer "legal
and political consequences."
This after The New York Times published a story that said her campaign recruited a candidate
with the same name as her Republican opponent.
The report relies on text messages that appear to show Peltola's campaign coordinated with
operatives to recruit a retired schoolteacher named Dan J. Sullivan to run for the seat
currently held by Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan.
NPR has not independently confirmed the Times reporting Democrats in the Peltola campaign
have denied that they had anything to do with his candidacy.
In Minnesota, prosecutors have charged right-wing provocateur James O'Keefe and another man
for misrepresenting their identities at polling places during the state's August primary
election from Minnesota Public Radio John Collins reports.
Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty says O'Keefe and fellow right-wing influencer
Cam Higby visited polling places around Minneapolis on August 11.
The men filmed themselves dressed in hijabs and spoke in accidents.
They said in videos posted online that they were testing the state's vouching system,
which allows registered voters to vouch for a neighbor on election day.
O'Keefe and Higby each faced felonies for identity theft and unlawful voting.
Moriarty says their actions violated state election law, even though they didn't cast
ballots.
There was no immediate comment from either Higby or O'Keefe, who are due in court next
month.
For NPR News, I'm John Collins in Minneapolis.
Flavio Bolsonaro, who lost Brazil's presidential election earlier this week, issued a statement

Bolsonaro and his family arrived in Miami today after he refused to concede the election
to incumbent president Luis Inacio Lula da Silva.
President Trump has also questioned Brazil's election result.
Bolsonaro is under investigation for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion.
His father is Jair Bolsonaro, who is in prison for plotting a coup after he lost the 2022
election.
U.S. stocks ticked higher today.
This is NPR News from Washington.
The U.N. General Assembly has condemned the U.S. economic embargo of Cuba for the 34th
year.
It comes even as Washington's campaign to influence the outcome led to a number of countries
voting against the resolution or sitting out of the decision for the first time.
The vote was 130-17 with 25 abstentions.
King Charles and Queen Camilla are on a nine-day tour of former British colonies in the Caribbean.
Protesters have gathered at some of his events demanding reparations for slavery during the
British empire, and Paris-Laurent Freire reports.
At a youth rally in the Bahamas, King Charles said the country's culture was born out of
darkness.
It is only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering and injustices of the
past.
But the monarch stopped short of apologizing for how his royal ancestors presided over and
profited from shipping millions of enslaved Africans to the Caribbean.
The issue of reparations is expected to come up at a Commonwealth summit starting Sunday
in Antigua, which the king is attending.
The secretary general of that group of mostly former British colonies has said the "time
has come for a discussion about compensation."
The royals have previously expressed sorrow for the past but ruled out reparations.
Lauren Freire, NPR News, London.

high fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark.
The MV Odyssey sent sail two years ago, marketed as a floating home for long-term living.
